fixes.explanation: Yes, friend, it's true. Agur says there are three things never satisfied, four that never say ‘Enough!’ Then he lists them: “Sheol, the barren womb, land never satisfied with water, and fire that never says, ‘Enough!’” He starts with three and lists four.
This one is true. Agur says, “Do not slander a servant to his master, or he will curse you, and you will bear the guilt.” It's a warning, and the guilt it names is yours. So the statement holds up.

That's right, baker. Agur says, “…there is a generation whose teeth are swords and whose jaws are knives, devouring the oppressed from the earth and the needy from among men.” It's a hard picture. The ones being devoured are the oppressed and the needy.

Kings and princes aren't named here. Agur says they are “…devouring the oppressed from the earth and the needy from among men.” The ones on the receiving end are the oppressed and the needy. It's a heavy line.

Jackals aren't in this verse. Agur says, “…may the ravens of the valley pluck it out and young vultures devour it.” The birds he names are ravens and young vultures. It's a heavy picture, and I think it hurts to read.
Danger isn't the word he uses. Agur says, “There are three things too wonderful for me, four that I cannot understand…” The word he gives is wonderful.
That's right, baker. Agur says, “This is the way of an adulteress: She eats and wipes her mouth and says, ‘I have done nothing wrong.’” She says she has done nothing wrong. It's a serious picture.
That's the opposite of what Agur says. He says she “…eats and wipes her mouth and says, ‘I have done nothing wrong.’” No sorry in sight. What she says is that she has done nothing wrong.
Yes, friend. Agur's list ends with “…a maidservant who supplants her mistress.” That's the fourth thing the earth cannot bear up under. It comes right after an unloved woman who marries.

Agur doesn't say that about the ants. He says, “The ants are creatures of little strength, yet they store up their food in the summer…” The wise thing he names is storing up food in summer. A leader isn't mentioned.
Yes, friend. Agur says, “…the locusts have no king, yet they all advance in formation…” No king, and they still advance in formation. That's the kind of order I'd love in my kitchen.
This one is true, friend. Agur says, “…the locusts have no king, yet they all advance in formation…” No king, and they still advance in formation. FALSE? The locusts would like a word.

City gates aren't in this verse. Agur says the lizard “…is found in the palaces of kings.” It can be caught in one’s hands, and that's still where it's found. Meanwhile I can't get through a phone menu without pressing zero five times.

Prophets aren't named here. Agur's fourth is “…a king with his army around him.” The first three are a lion, a strutting rooster and a he-goat, so the king and his army walk in that company. A rooster in that lineup gets me every time.
Shame isn't what Agur says. He says, “…so the stirring of anger brings forth strife.” Each action gives its result. Stirring anger gives strife.
